bio: Su Tung-p’o (Su Shi, 1036–1101) was one of the foremost poets of the Sung dynasty. Waley includes his well-known humorous quatrain written on the birth of a son.
The poems here are Arthur Waley’s version in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918), given with the poet’s name as spelled in those books.

poems.title: On the Birth of his Son
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.collection: A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918)
poems.text:
Families, when a child is born
Want it to be intelligent.
I, through intelligence,
Having wrecked my whole life,
Only hope the baby will prove
Ignorant and stupid.
Then he will crown a tranquil life
By becoming a Cabinet Minister.

poems.title: Spring Nights
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.text:
One half-hour of a night in spring is worth a thousand taels,
When the clear sweet scent of flowers is felt and the moon her lustre pales;
When mellowed sounds of song and flute are borne along the breeze,
And through the stilly scene the swing sounds swishing from the trees.

poems.title: Whigs and Tories
poems.author: Su Tung-p’o
poems.text:
Thickly o'er the jasper terrace flower shadows play;
In vain I call my garden boy to sweep them all away.
They vanish when the sun sets in the west, but very soon
They spring to giddy life again beneath the rising moon!
